name: Modular reciprocating engine power plants
principle: Power plants built from factory-fabricated modules: an engine, generator and auxiliaries are assembled and tested in a factory enclosure (a genset container or a multi-megawatt power block), shipped complete and bolted together on a prepared foundation, with no site welding. Wärtsilä's Modular Block takes one 34SG generating set per block, Rolls-Royce (mtu) offers factory-tested 10, 20 and 30 MW power blocks for plants of five to several hundred megawatts, and Everllence (formerly MAN Energy Solutions) modularises engine-specific systems for its 51/60 series plants.

advantages: Build time of about a year to 18 months from order, against several years for a large thermal station
Capacity added engine by engine, so output scales with demand and one engine outage costs little
Factory quality control and testing before shipment; no site welding
Fast start (about two minutes for a 34SG) suits balancing and data-centre backup duty
limitations: Per-engine ratings top out around 10-20 MW, so very large plants need many units
Single-cycle efficiency near 51% stays below a large combined cycle at over 60%
Higher maintenance intensity per MWh than turbine plant

gaps.item: capital cost per kW for a modular engine plant versus a conventional build, with dollar year
gaps.reason: Searched three times (2026-10-28, 2026-11-16 twice). No open source states a capital cost per kW for a modular/containerised engine plant, or a premium/discount against a stick-built plant: EIA's AEO2025 capital-cost report has no reciprocating-engine or modular line to cite, the Danish Energy Agency catalogue page 404s, ESMAP's equipment-price study is 403, and vendor pages claim only qualitative savings (Wärtsilä's '20-30% lower CAPEX' names no comparator). The EPA and DOE engine figures now on pwr-gas-engines are engine CHP, not a modular premium.

where.hint: Manufacturer investor material or EPC tender results comparing modular and stick-built engine plants
Owner/utility board papers publishing both bids for the same project

gaps.action: Treat as unmeasured. Only an owner/utility board paper publishing both bids for one project, or a manufacturer's investor disclosure, can close this; do not derive it by subtracting unrelated figures.

gaps.reason: No agency assigns a TRL or maturity grade to modular engine plants as distinct from the engine itself: the IEA Clean Energy Technology Guide dataset has no such row, and maturity schemes (IEA, DOE, EPA) grade reciprocating/gas engines generically. Commercial deployment is evidenced by the reference plants (Dohazari 102 MW in 10 months; KPUB 124 MW), so the blocker is the missing agency rating, not the technology.

where.hint: IEA ETP Clean Energy Technology Guide (collected): search for reciprocating engine power plants

gaps.action: Leave the TRL empty rather than infer 9; cite the deployment record in prose if a number is demanded.

notes: MAN Energy Solutions was renamed Everllence on 4 June 2025 (everllence.com press release read 26 October 2026); the catalogued source record still carries the former name. Rolls-Royce Power Systems launched its modular gas engine power plant offer in February 2026, so the concept is new even though mtu gensets have run on the UK grid since 2014. Wärtsilä reports 81 GW of engine power plant capacity delivered (wartsila.com/energy/engine-power-plant-solutions, read 26 October 2026). Deployment sequence provenance: factory fabrication and testing, bolted site erection without welding and the ~5-week assembly window are as described in Wärtsilä's Modular Block article (wartsila.com/insights/article/towards-higher-efficiencies-with-wartsila-modular-block, read 2026-11-16); balance-of-plant and grid-synchronisation steps are the standard plant sequence.
